knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", message = FALSE)

# Introduction

`spatialLagGLM` asks, gene by gene, whether the expression at a spot is
associated with the expression at the spots around it, in spatial
transcriptomics data stored in a `SpatialExperiment`. For each gene it fits a
quasi-Poisson regression with a library-size offset, optional design terms
from `colData`, and the *spatial lag* of the gene's own normalised counts as
an extra covariate. The lag coefficient, its p-value and its adjusted p-value
are written to `rowData()` of the input object.

## Relation to existing packages

Several methods already find spatially variable genes (SVGs). SPARK-X
[Zhu et al. 2021], nnSVG [Weber et al. 2023] and SpatialDE
[Svensson et al. 2018] test whether
a gene's expression has spatial covariance structure, using kernel or Gaussian
process models, and they target any spatial pattern. Moran's I is the
classical autocorrelation statistic.

`spatialLagGLM` is a simpler regression-style alternative. What it offers is:

* results stored in the `SpatialExperiment` you pass in;
* a `design` formula, so that the lag is tested while adjusting for
  `colData` variables such as a cluster or condition;
* neighbours defined within each sample separately, so multi-sample objects
  are handled directly.

What it does not offer is the statistical track record of the methods above.
The p-values come from a quasi-Poisson fit that has not been shown to be
calibrated for this test (see [Checking calibration] and [Limitations]). If
you need a well-established SVG test, use one of the packages above; use
`spatialLagGLM` for exploratory screening and for design-adjusted lag
estimates, and confirm hits independently.

# Installation

```{r install, eval = FALSE}
if (!requireNamespace("BiocManager", quietly = TRUE)) {
    install.packages("BiocManager")
}
BiocManager::install("spatialLagGLM")
```

# The model

For one gene, let $y_i$ be the count at spot $i$. The model is

$$\log E[y_i] = \log(s_i) + X_i\beta + \gamma\, l_i,
\qquad l_i = \sum_j w_{ij}\,\frac{y_j}{s_j},$$

fitted with a quasi-Poisson family. Here $s_i$ is the size factor of spot $i$
(library size divided by the geometric mean of library sizes), $X_i$ is the
row of the design matrix, and $w_{ij}$ are weights: the inverse distance
between spots $i$ and $j$ if they are within `radius` of each other (and in
the same sample), zero otherwise, with each row scaled to sum to one. A spot
with no neighbours has $l_i = 0$.

The **null hypothesis** is $\gamma = 0$: given the offset and the design
terms, the expression at a spot is not associated with the weighted mean of
the normalised expression of its neighbours. The **effect size** reported is
$\hat\gamma$.

Because $l_i$ is built from the same gene's counts, this is **not** a spatial
autoregressive (SAR) model.

# Input data

The package ships a simulated dataset: a 30 x 30 grid of spots and 50 genes.
Spots within 7 units of the centre are labelled `TumorCore`, the rest
`Margin`. `Gene1` is up-regulated in the core; the other 49 genes are
simulated without any spatial pattern.

```{r mock}
library(spatialLagGLM)
library(SpatialExperiment)
set.seed(1)
se <- makeMockSpatial()
se
table(se$condition)
```

The function needs a `SpatialExperiment` with a raw-count assay, spatial
coordinates, and a `sample_id` column in `colData` (which every
`SpatialExperiment` has). Spots with zero total counts must be removed
first.

# Running the analysis

```{r run-condition}
res <- spatialLagGLM(se, design = ~condition, radius = 2.5)
head(SummarizedExperiment::rowData(res), 3)
```

## Arguments

`design`
: A formula using `colData` variables, e.g. `~ condition`. Use `~ 1` for no
  adjustment. With `~ condition`, the lag is tested after allowing a
  different mean in each condition, so a pattern that is fully explained by
  `condition` is *not* reported. Compare:

```{r run-intercept}
res0 <- spatialLagGLM(se, design = ~1, radius = 2.5)
rd <- SummarizedExperiment::rowData
cols <- c("spatial_effect_size", "p_value")
out <- rbind(
    as.data.frame(rd(res)["Gene1", cols]),
    as.data.frame(rd(res0)["Gene1", cols])
)
rownames(out) <- c("~ condition", "~ 1")
out
```

`radius`
: A positive number: the distance within which spots count as neighbours, in
  the units of `spatialCoords(se)`. See [Choosing the radius].

`assay.type`
: The assay holding raw counts (default `"counts"`).

`size.factors`
: Optional. By default size factors come from the library sizes of the assay
  you pass in. If you subset genes before the analysis, pass size factors
  computed from all genes (see the real-data example).

`BPPARAM`
: A `BiocParallelParam`, e.g. `BiocParallel::MulticoreParam(4)`. Genes are
  fitted in parallel.

## Several samples

Weights are computed separately for each value of `colData(se)$sample_id`,
so spots in different sections are never neighbours. All samples are assumed
to share the same coordinate units, because one `radius` is used for all.

# Output

The input object is returned with three new columns in `rowData()`:

`spatial_effect_size`
: $\hat\gamma$, the change in the log expected count per unit increase in the
  neighbours' weighted mean normalised count. Positive means a spot tends to
  be high where its neighbours are high.

`p_value`
: The quasi-Poisson t-test p-value for $\gamma = 0$.

`adjusted_p_value`
: Benjamini-Hochberg adjustment of `p_value` across genes.

`NA` is returned for genes whose fit failed or did not converge, and a warning
reports how many. The radius, assay and size factors used are kept in
`S4Vectors::metadata(res)$spatialLagGLM`.

Two points on interpretation. First, the effect size is in units of
normalised counts, so it depends on how highly a gene is expressed: a
highly expressed gene has a smaller $\hat\gamma$ for the same relative
pattern. Compare genes by p-value, not by effect size, and treat the effect
size cutoff in the volcano plot as a display choice. Second, the p-values are
exploratory (see below).

# Plots

`plotSpatialLag()` draws a gene on the tissue coordinates, either as raw
counts or as its spatial lag (the covariate used in the model).

```{r plot-expression, fig.height = 4, fig.width = 5}
plotSpatialLag(res0, "Gene1", metric = "expression")
```

```{r plot-lag, fig.height = 4, fig.width = 5}
plotSpatialLag(res0, "Gene1", metric = "spatial_lag")
```

`plotLagVolcano()` shows effect size against adjusted p-value for all genes.

```{r volcano, fig.height = 4, fig.width = 5}
plotLagVolcano(res0)
```

An interactive explorer combining both is available with
`runSpatialLagExplorer(res0)` (requires the `shiny` package).

# Choosing the radius

`radius` sets the scale at which neighbours are defined. Too small and many
spots have no neighbours; too large and the lag becomes a smooth regional
average. A practical starting point is a small multiple of the typical
nearest-neighbour distance. On the mock grid, spots are one unit apart, so
`radius = 1.5` includes the 8 surrounding spots and `radius = 2.5` the 20
nearest.

```{r radius}
coords <- spatialCoords(se)
d <- as.matrix(dist(coords))
diag(d) <- Inf
median(apply(d, 1, min))
```

It is worth checking that conclusions do not change much over a few
radii:

```{r radius-sens}
p_by_radius <- vapply(c(1.5, 2.5, 4), function(r) {
    out <- spatialLagGLM(se, design = ~1, radius = r)
    rd(out)["Gene1", "p_value"]
}, numeric(1))
names(p_by_radius) <- c(1.5, 2.5, 4)
p_by_radius
```

# Example on real data

This example uses a 10x Visium sample of human dorsolateral prefrontal
cortex from the `STexampleData` package. To keep the vignette fast we analyse
the 300 most highly expressed genes. Because `spatialLagGLM()` derives size
factors from the genes it is given, we compute them first from *all* genes and
pass them in.

```{r real-load, eval = has_ste}
library(STexampleData)
spe <- Visium_humanDLPFC()
spe <- spe[, as.logical(spe$in_tissue)]
counts_all <- SummarizedExperiment::assay(spe, "counts")
spe <- spe[, colSums(counts_all) > 0]

counts_all <- SummarizedExperiment::assay(spe, "counts")
lib <- colSums(counts_all)
sf <- lib / exp(mean(log(lib)))

top <- order(rowSums(counts_all), decreasing = TRUE)[seq_len(300)]
spe <- spe[top, ]
dim(spe)
```

The coordinates are in image pixels. We set the radius to 1.5 times the
median nearest-neighbour distance, which captures the first ring of
neighbours on the Visium hexagonal grid.

```{r real-radius, eval = has_ste}
xy <- spatialCoords(spe)
d <- as.matrix(dist(xy))
diag(d) <- Inf
radius <- 1.5 * median(apply(d, 1, min))
radius
```

```{r real-run, eval = has_ste}
res_real <- spatialLagGLM(
    spe,
    design = ~1, radius = radius, size.factors = sf,
    BPPARAM = BiocParallel::SerialParam()
)
tab <- as.data.frame(
    SummarizedExperiment::rowData(res_real)[, c(
        "spatial_effect_size", "p_value", "adjusted_p_value"
    )]
)
head(tab[order(tab$p_value), ], 5)
```

```{r real-plot, eval = has_ste, fig.height = 4, fig.width = 5}
top_gene <- rownames(tab)[which.min(tab$p_value)]
plotSpatialLag(res_real, top_gene, metric = "spatial_lag")
```

# Checking calibration

The quasi-Poisson p-values have not been shown to be calibrated for this
test, so check them on your data. The mock data gives a first look: genes 2
to 50 have no spatial pattern, so under a calibrated test about 5% of their
p-values would fall below 0.05.

```{r calib, fig.height = 3.5, fig.width = 5}
null_p <- rd(res0)$p_value[-1]
mean(null_p < 0.05)
hist(null_p,
    breaks = 20, main = "Genes 2-50 (no spatial pattern)",
    xlab = "p-value"
)
```

In a simulation by the package author (independent negative binomial genes on
this grid, design `~ 1`, 40 replicates), about 18% of null p-values were below
0.05. The p-values are therefore **anti-conservative** and a small p-value
should not be read as 0.05-level evidence.

A permutation null gives an empirical reference. Permuting the spots
(columns) of the count matrix keeps each spot's library size but breaks any
link between expression and location. Running the method on permuted data
shows what p-values to expect from no spatial signal:

```{r perm}
perm_counts <- SummarizedExperiment::assay(se, "counts")[, sample(ncol(se))]
colnames(perm_counts) <- colnames(se)
perm <- se
SummarizedExperiment::assay(perm, "counts") <- perm_counts
res_perm <- spatialLagGLM(perm, design = ~1, radius = 2.5)
perm_p <- rd(res_perm)$p_value
obs_p <- rd(res0)$p_value

mean(perm_p < 0.05)
## Empirical p-value: how often a permuted gene is at least as extreme.
emp_p <- vapply(
    obs_p, function(p) {
        (1 + sum(perm_p <= p)) / (1 + length(perm_p))
    },
    numeric(1)
)
emp_p["Gene1"]
```

With only 50 genes the permutation null is coarse. With a full dataset, pool
several permutations and use the pooled p-values the same way.

# Limitations

* The p-values are exploratory and anti-conservative in simulation. Confirm
  hits with an established SVG method and a permutation null.
* The model is not a spatial autoregressive model; it regresses a gene on the
  lag of its own counts.
* Effect sizes depend on expression level and are not comparable across genes.
* The results depend on `radius`.
* Counts are converted to a dense matrix. Datasets with many tens of
  thousands of spots will need a lot of memory.
